sections.heading: Dialogue II, Knot iv, part 2 (printed pp. 170–173)
rows: Ereu. De primo non refert, ait enim causas minus principales (quales sunt littorum & fundorum maris diversae species) quoad motus terminos magis esse efficaces quam ipsammet praecipuam. Quomodo autem hoc operentur adhuc incompertum asserit. Immo non ultra Mediterraneum hoc contingere credit, quantumvis nulla notior de Oceano experientia nobis constet.

Ereu. Of the first it does not matter [non refert]; for he says that the less principal causes (such as are the diverse forms [species] of the shores and of the bottoms of the sea), as regards the terms [terminos] of the motion, are more efficacious than the principal [cause] itself. But how they work [operentur] this, he asserts [to be] as yet unascertained [incompertum]. Nay, he believes that this does not happen beyond the Mediterranean, however much no better-known experience [experientia] concerning the Ocean is established [constet] for us.

Circa menstruum motum notat lunam modo intra nos & solem modo extra videri. Unde conicit terrae accidere quod in horologio, ut luna (ponderum vice) motum telluris cum a sole longinquior est, retardet, cum propinquior est acceleret, & non considerat quod praeterquam haec coniectura pura sit, neque instituto ipsius serviat cum idem sit effectus circa mare & cum longinquissima est luna, & cum propinquissima: in utroque enim casu aestus crescit. Deinde ipsemet inaequalitatem hanc motus terrae per menses nondum esse animadversam, confitetur.

About the monthly motion he notes that the moon is seen now within [intra] us and the sun, now outside. Whence he conjectures that there befalls the earth what [befalls] in a clock [horologio], that the moon (in the place [vice] of the weights) retards the motion of the earth [telluris] when it is farther from the sun, accelerates [it] when it is nearer; and he does not consider that, besides [the fact] that this is pure conjecture, neither does it serve his purpose [instituto], since the effect about the sea is the same both when the moon is farthest and when nearest: for in either case the tide [aestus] grows. Next, he himself confesses that this inequality of the motion of the earth through the months has not yet been noticed [animadversam].

Circa annuum motum notat terram sub Zodiaco motam habere motum diurnum, interdum magis conformem motui annuo, interdum minus, secundum quod axis terrae semper versus Polos Aequatoris fixus magis accedit ad naturam tangentis Eclipticae vel recedit ab ea, & verum est videri accelerari per hoc cursum terrae annuum circa aequinoctia: [p. 171] retardari circa solstitia; sed utrum in mare aliquem effectum habeat non adeo constat, & alterius disputationis est.

About the annual motion he notes that the earth, moved under the Zodiac, has a daily motion sometimes more conformable to the annual motion, sometimes less, according as [secundum quod] the axis of the earth, always fixed towards the Poles of the Equator, approaches more to the nature of a tangent of the Ecliptic, or recedes from it; and it is true that through this the annual course of the earth seems to be accelerated about the equinoxes, [p. 171] to be retarded about the solstices; but whether it has any effect on [in] the sea is not so [adeo] certain [constat], and is [matter] of another disputation.
Andab. Huius, si placet Ereuni, aut me in tenebris relinquis.
Andab. Of this [huius] [give me an account], if it pleases [you], Ereunius, or [else] you leave me in darkness.

Ereu. Satis credo te intelligere tellurem sub Ecliptica volutam simul Eclipticae partem decurrere, cum diurna sui permutatione. Eclipticam autem hic vides in aequinoctiis cum Aequatore coire; in solstitiis maxime disiungi, quod si in sphaera materiali consideres, reperias perpetuam respectuum inter eos circulos novitatem: sed habesne apud te, Asphali, sphaeram, vel globum?

Ereu. I believe you understand sufficiently that the earth [tellurem], rolled under the Ecliptic, at the same time runs down [decurrere] a part of the Ecliptic, together with the daily change [permutatione] of itself. But the Ecliptic you see here to come together with the Equator at the equinoxes; at the solstices to be most disjoined; which if you consider [it] on a material sphere [sphaera materiali], you would find a perpetual newness of the relations [respectuum] between those circles: but have you with you, Asphalius, a sphere or a globe?
Asphal. Habeo & ecce proxime Andabatam scrinium, & in scrinio clavem, eam si verteris, accipies quod maxime libuerit.
Asphal. I have [one]; and behold, very near Andabata, a cabinet [scrinium], and in the cabinet a key: if you turn it, you will receive whatever most pleases [you].
Andab. Ecce sphaeram, ea si ad rem tuam fecerit, utere: Globorum enim difficilior est translatio.
Andab. Behold a sphere; if it will serve [fecerit ad] your matter, use it: for the carrying-across [translatio] of globes is more difficult.

Ereu. Sphaerae ratio aptior est, huius praesertim quae ipsamet est quam meo iussu curavisti fieri, Asphali, cum Copernicaeum motum aliquando repraesentari a me posceres. Vide itaque, Andabata, quomodo hic telluris axis qui parallelus est axi Aequatoris semper in revolutione novam acquirat inclinationem, & hic in aequinoctiis parallelus sit axi Aequatoris, in solstitiis perpendicularis.

Ereu. The plan [ratio] of a sphere is more apt, especially of this one, which is the very one which by my order you had made [curavisti fieri], Asphalius, when you once [aliquando] demanded that the Copernican motion be represented by me. See then, Andabata, how here the axis of the earth [telluris], which is parallel to the axis of the Equator, always in the revolution acquires a new inclination, and here at the equinoxes is parallel to the axis of the Equator, at the solstices perpendicular.
[p. 172] Andab. Video.
[p. 172] Andab. I see.
Ereu. Et advertis motum ipsius terrae super suum axem esse sub Ecliptica?
Ereu. And do you notice [advertis] that the motion of the earth itself upon its own axis is under the Ecliptic?
Andab. Etiam hoc video.
Andab. This too I see.

Ereu. Vides itaque cursum telluris diurnum in aequinoctiis cum Ecliptica convenire, in solstitiis prorsus diversum esse, in intervallis plus minusve accedere, quo his punctis magis vel minus applicatur.

Ereu. You see then that the daily course of the earth [telluris] at the equinoxes agrees [convenire] with the Ecliptic, at the solstices is altogether different, in the intervals approaches more or less, by as much as [quo] it is applied more or less to these points.
Andab. Hoc etiam clarum est.
Andab. This also is clear.

Ereu. Si itaque a duabus causis proficiscuntur hi motus, velocior ex necessitate erit motus telluris in aequinoctiis, tardior in solstitiis: Et hoc existimavit Galilaeus. Sin una utriusque est causa, nihilo velocior erit motus sive diurnus sive annuus.

Ereu. If then these motions proceed from two causes, the motion of the earth [telluris] will of necessity be swifter at the equinoxes, slower at the solstices: And this Galileo thought. But if there is one cause of both, the motion, whether daily or annual, will be swifter by nothing [nihilo].
Andab. Quid enim interest ab una an pluribus causis proficiscatur hoc effectum?
Andab. For what difference does it make whether this [thing] effected [hoc effectum] proceeds from one or from several causes?
Ereu. Examinandae sunt prius motuum causae, quam ut hunc nodum clare dirimere valeam.
Ereu. The causes of the motions must be examined first, before [prius … quam ut] I can clearly cut apart [dirimere] this knot [nodum].

Andab. Etiamsi tuo Galilaeo propter errores quos tenet, iniquior sim, non possum tamen tam excultam & subtilem machinam, quam aestui explicando fabricavit, non admirari, & dolere non eventu digno esse cumulatam. Utcumque est, tibi, Ereuni, gratulor, qui hanc terrae mobilitatem sustulisti, in quam tot magna ingenia misere impingen- [p. 173] tia naufragium fecerunt.

Andab. Even if I be rather unfavourable [iniquior] to your Galileo on account of the errors which he holds, yet I cannot not admire so finely-wrought [excultam] and subtle a machine [machinam] as he fabricated for explaining the tide [aestui], and [cannot not] grieve that it has not been crowned [cumulatam] with a worthy outcome [eventu]. However it be, I congratulate you, Ereunius, who have removed [sustulisti] this mobility of the earth, upon which so many great wits [ingenia], wretchedly striking [impingen-|[p. 173] tia], have made shipwreck.
Ereu. Immerito (meam fidem) gratulatus es neque feci enim, neque dixi, neque cogitavi.
Ereu. Undeservedly (upon my faith [meam fidem]) you have congratulated [me]; for neither have I done [it], nor said [it], nor thought [it].
Andab. Saltem hoc perfecisti posse sine motu terrae consistere maris fluxum & refluxum.
Andab. At least this you have accomplished [perfecisti]: that the flux and reflux of the sea can subsist [consistere] without motion of the earth.
Ereu. Neque hoc ex me audivisti.
Ereu. Neither have you heard this from me.
Andab. Quid itaque hoc longo discursu egisti?
Andab. What then have you done [egisti] by this long discourse [discursu]?
Ereu. Tuae admirationi satisfeci, & conatus sum ostendere motum telluris non esse mari causam aestuandi.
Ereu. I have satisfied your wonder [admirationi], and have tried to show that the motion of the earth [telluris] is not for the sea the cause of tiding [aestuandi].
Andab. Ludis me, non hoc tantumdem est? si enim causa non est, Aestus citra ipsius existentiam consistere potest.
Andab. You are mocking me; is this not just as much [tantumdem]? for if it is not the cause, the Tide can subsist [consistere] without [citra] its existence.

terms: it is of no consequence; (lit.) it brings nothing back
Ereunius dismisses Galileo's daily period (the 'first' of the terms of the tides) because Galileo himself credits secondary causes.
Continues part 1: the periods (daily, monthly, annual) at which the tides recur.
Here not the scholastic 'species' but the shapes of coasts and sea-beds, Galileo's secondary causes.
Galileo's admission (Dialogo IV) that the working of secondary causes is not yet understood.
the moon in the place of the weights / clock
pendulum or regulator weights of a clock
Galileo's analogy: moving weights along a clock's balance-rod speeds or slows it; the moon's distance from the sun would modulate the earth's annual speed.
i.e. at conjunction (new moon); 'extra' = at opposition (full moon).
in so far as, in proportion as
the nature of a tangent of the Ecliptic
Galileo's account of the annual (equinoctial/solstitial) inequality from the composition of diurnal and annual motions.
A physical model of the celestial circles, distinguished from a globe.
Scholastic 'respectus' = relation; here the changing angular relations of circles.
Domestic stage-business: the sphere is fetched from Asphalius' cabinet.
The bulky globe is harder to fetch.
Ratio as the constructive scheme of the instrument.
Asphalius had commissioned an armillary sphere showing Copernicus' system.
Neuter effectum where elsewhere White uses masc. effectus.
A pun on the book's division into nodi; the question is deferred to later analysis of causes.
Galileo's tide-theory as an engineered 'machine' (cf. glossary: machina).
Not crowned with a worthy result = not borne out.
Nautical metaphor fitting the subject of tides; the earth's mobility as a reef.
Here = discourse, not the 'running-about' of planets (glossary).
Gerund 'causa aestuandi' = cause of [the sea's] tiding.
on this side of; short of; without
Andabata takes 'not the cause' to imply 'tide possible without earth's motion'; Ereunius (next knot) will distinguish.
notes: Unit: Dialogue II, Knot iv, part 2 of 2 (completes the knot). PDF pp. 181–184 = printed pp. 170–173, from ‘Ereu. De primo non refert’ (p. 170) to Andabata's ‘…Aestus citra ipsius existentiam consistere potest.’ (p. 173). Knot v begins on p. 173 with ‘Ereu. Siccine arbitraris?’, beside the margin ‘Nodus V. Nullam esse resistentiam in terra ad motum’ (FM2 table: ‘Nullam esse resistentiam terrae ad motum’, p. 173). Offset +11 holds (signatures Y ij p. 171, Y iij p. 173). No marginal notes occur in this part's text.

Uncertain readings / interpretations: (a) p. 171 ‘Huius, si placet Ereuni, aut me in tenebris relinquis.’ — elliptical; a verb (e.g. ‘fac me participem’ / ‘rationem redde’) is understood; supplied as ‘[give me an account]’. (b) p. 171 ‘& hic in aequinoctiis parallelus sit axi Aequatoris, in solstitiis perpendicularis’ — read clearly as printed, but astronomically puzzling since the earth's axis was just said to be always parallel to the Equator's axis; White probably means the axis's changing relation to the tangent of the Ecliptic (the direction of the annual motion) as seen on the sphere; the text as printed is kept and translated literally. (c) p. 170 ‘lunam’ is followed by a stray mark (‘lunam' modo’), ignored. (d) p. 173 ‘gratulatus es neque feci enim’ — no stop after ‘es’, and ‘enim’ in third position; punctuated in the English. (e) p. 172 ‘Galilęus’ normalised Galilaeus. (f) p. 171 ‘ea si ad rem tuam fecerit, utere’ — ‘ea’ read as ablative with ‘utere’ (and subject of ‘fecerit’).

Verification pass (sentence by sentence against the Latin and the page images; margin of p. 173 re-read on a 300 dpi crop): no omissions or additions found; 3 corrections — (1) p. 170 ‘intra nos & solem’ first drafted ‘within us’ alone; corrected to keep ‘us and the sun’ together as the object of intra (= between us and the sun); (2) p. 172 ‘quo his punctis magis vel minus applicatur’ — ‘quo’ corrected from ‘where’ to ‘by as much as’ (correlative degree); (3) p. 172 ‘non possum … non admirari, & dolere’ — the negated ‘non possum’ made to govern ‘dolere’ as well (‘[cannot not] grieve’). Remaining uncertainties as listed above.
